title: The Cedar Mountain, dwelling of the gods
short: The Cedar Mountain is 'the home of the Immortals, shrine of Irnini': the forest belongs to the gods.
body: George translates 'the dwelling of the gods, the throne-dais of Irnini'. The sanctity of the place means that felling its trees is not only adventure but sacrilege, at least from Enlil's point of view. The heroes stand in awe at the forest's edge, admiring its height and shade: a moment of stillness before the violence. Thompson's 'home of th' Immortals' renders the same phrase. The heroes' stopping and staring is a moment of wonder that some critics compare with the first sight of a sacred grove in classical literature.

title: Irnini
short: Irnini is a name of Ishtar: the Cedar Mountain is her sanctuary.
body: Thompson's note: 'A form of Ishtar.' The link anticipates Tablet VI, where Ishtar, having watched the victorious Gilgamish, proposes to him. Ishtar's association with mountain sanctuaries in the west is attested elsewhere. Ishtar had many names and local forms; Irnini was one used in poetry and hymns. Calling the Cedar Mountain her 'shrine' makes the attack on the forest an intrusion into the domain of the goddess who will soon desire the victor. George discusses the name in his commentary on the passage, and notes that the forest's sanctity is a recurring theme of Tablet V.

title: The Cedar Forest as a noisy jungle: the Sulaymaniyah tablet
short: A tablet acquired by the Sulaymaniyah Museum in 2011 adds lines describing the forest full of monkeys, cicadas and birds.
body: Al-Rawi and George (2014) published a new manuscript of Tablet V that fills the gap after Thompson's 'Fair was its shade'. The forest is a dense jungle whose animal noises form a kind of music for Humbaba, which makes him look more like a foreign ruler entertained at his court than a simple brute. The tablet also adds that, after the killing, Enkidu acknowledges they have reduced the forest to a wasteland, which sharpens the moral ambiguity. This discovery came almost ninety years after Thompson's translation.

title: The dreams on the road to the Forest
short: Gilgamish's dreams of a falling mountain and a storm are terrifying; Enkidu always interprets them as signs of victory.
body: In George's Tablet IV there are five dreams, and in each Enkidu gives a favourable interpretation (the mountain is Humbaba, who will fall). Many readers find the interpretations forced; the dreams seem to foretell disaster, not least Enkidu's own death. Thompson's restorations here are 'obviously uncertain', as he notes. The pattern of dreams and readings links back to Nin-sun's interpretations in Tablet I.

title: The stages of the journey
short: The repeated stages ('at the fortieth league ... at the sixtieth') belong to a formula repeated at each day of the journey.
body: See the note on leagues in Tablet IV. The formula reappears at the end of Tablet XI on the journey home. Repetition marks the passage of time and the immense distances covered in a few days by superhuman travellers. In Thompson's version the stages are partly lost; George's edition restores the formula for each of the six days of travel, with a well dug and a dream sought at every halt. The fortieth and sixtieth leagues of Thompson's line correspond to a different reading of the numbers.

anchor: Mountain, a dream do thou grant
title: Asking the mountain for a dream
short: Gilgamish climbs a hill, pours out flour and asks the mountain to send a dream: an incubation ritual.
body: Seeking revelatory dreams by ritual (incubation) was a recognised practice in Mesopotamia. The offering of flour (Thompson's 'meal') and the crouching posture, chin on knees, are described each night of the journey in George's Tablet IV. Thompson's 'squatting bent-kneed' captures that posture. The mountain 'breathes' on him and a chill wind passes, signalling the divine presence. Each night the dream that follows is frightening, and each morning Enkidu interprets it favourably. The cycle structures the whole journey and builds suspense before the fight.

title: The third dream: storm and fire
short: In the most terrifying dream heaven roars, earth echoes, fire falls and Death is gorged: imagery of cosmic catastrophe.
body: The language of thunder, lightning and fire turning to ash anticipates the Flood narrative and Enkidu's dream of the underworld. Enkidu reads it as a sign of victory, but its images of death seem more ominous. Note also the motif of waking suddenly and asking 'Didst thou not call me?' which recurs when Gilgamish wakes from the long sleep in Tablet XI.

title: Shamash's winds
short: Shamash sends winds that pin Humbaba down; Thompson's text has eight, while George's has thirteen.
body: The Sun-god intervenes decisively, as Nin-sun had prayed: the winds blow into Humbaba's eyes so that he can neither advance nor retreat. George's edition, based on more manuscripts, lists thirteen winds. The motif resembles Marduk's use of the winds against Tiamat in Enuma Elish. The divine help diminishes the heroes' glory somewhat: they do not defeat Humbaba unaided. The number of winds varies between versions, a sign of how the text was expanded over time.

title: Humbaba's plea for mercy
short: Defeated, Humbaba begs to become Gilgamish's servant; Enkidu insists that he be killed.
body: In George's fuller text Humbaba offers to cut timber for Gilgamish and reminds Enkidu that he once knew him in the wild; when Enkidu urges his death, Humbaba curses them both, wishing that Enkidu not grow old. The killing despite the plea is morally troubling and leads to the gods' decision against Enkidu. Thompson's text preserves only the outline. Compare scenes in the Iliad where suppliants are refused (Lycaon, Iliad 21).

title: The head of Humbaba
short: The heroes cut off Humbaba's head; in George's text they take it, and a great cedar door, back down the Euphrates.
body: Thompson's tablet ends here. In George's edition the friends fell the forest, Enkidu makes a door for Enlil's temple at Nippur, and they raft the timber down the Euphrates, with Gilgamish carrying the head. In the Sumerian version the head is brought to Enlil, who is angry. The trophy marks the climax of Gilgamish's quest for fame, at the price of divine anger.
